meta.session_title: Day 1 - Introduction to Java & Language Fundamentals
meta.pedagogy: Hands-on learning with step-by-step guidance. Each exercise builds on the previous. All concepts from the session are coded. Banking/finance examples used for context.

objectives: Combine ALL Day 1 concepts in a single integrated program: primitives, operators, flow control, arrays, and best practices to build a complete mini banking application.
prerequisites: IntelliJ IDEA (Community Edition) or VS Code with Java Extension
Git installed and GitHub account created

exercises.title: Capstone Lab — Mini Bank Statement Generator
exercises.objective: Combine ALL Day 1 concepts in a single integrated program: primitives, operators, flow control, arrays, and best practices to build a complete mini banking application.
exercises.scenario: Build a mini bank statement generator for RoboBank. It processes an array of transactions, categorizes them, computes running balance, flags large transactions, and prints a formatted statement. This represents the kind of real code you'll write as a Java developer.
instructions: Step 2: Implement all sections — this is your Day 1 integration test
Step 3: Run and match expected output
Step 4: Add a feature: also count how many transactions are above ₹20,000
Step 5: Git commit your work: 'Day 1: Java fundamentals complete - primitives, operators, control flow, arrays'
hints: String.format("₹%,.2f", amount) formats a number with rupee symbol, comma separators, and 2 decimals.
Math.abs(txnAmt) gives the absolute value — useful to track debit amounts as positive numbers.
To print top 3 from sorted (ascending) array: loop from length-1 down to length-3.
reflection_questions: This program uses int, double, boolean, char, and String. Which Java primitive types did we NOT use here — and can you add a use case for each?
Why do we use static final constants instead of inline magic numbers?
If you had 10,000 transactions, would this approach still work? What would you change?
exercises.debugging_task: Intentionally remove the Math.abs() from totalDebit. What happens to the total debit amount? Why? This demonstrates why absolute value handling is critical in financial calculations.
